newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr vulnerable despite buying, U.S. dlr.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr vulnerable despite buying, U.S. dlr.

text.p: The Australian dollar touched a six week low on Monday, but was rescued from breaking the key US$0.7740 support by local buyers and the surging U.S. dollar which rose to a 50 month high of 125.00 yen in Tokyo.

The dollar had touched a low of US$0.7744 after heavy selling of the Aussie/yen cross near 96.50 yen in morning trade, but while it recovered from its lows it never left its danger zone and sentiment still remains bearish, traders said.
At 4.30 p.m. (0630 GMT) the unit was at US$0.7754/59 from an early US$0.7759/64 and a local Friday close of US$0.7760/65.
The dollar had risen as high as US$0.7769 in the afternoon, but there had been selling interest throughout that eventually soaked up demand.

While a squeeze higher towards US$0.7780/7800 was still possible, traders said offshore appeared ready to sell into any rally, while exporters and local institutions were for the moment happy to buy from around US$0.7750.
The lack of a convincing bounce in the Australian dollar since it fell through US$0.7800 last Thursday has added to the prevailing negative market tone.

The early selling on the Aussie/yen cross was led by offshore sellers. However, the continuing strength of the U.S. dollar, despite the release of an increase in Japan's trade surplus, saw the Australian dollar dragged higher.

The Australian dollar ended at 96.68/78 yen from an opening 96.44/54 and a Friday close of 95.82/92. It had traded as high as 97.04 yen as the U.S. dollar reached 125.00, its highest level since February 1993, but traders said there were sellers at this level.
In trade weighted terms the local dollar closed at 59.9, up on an opening 59.8 and a previous close of 59.7.
The weakness of the dollar is in line with what many analysts had expected when the U.S lifted rates last month, a move that was seen as the first of at least two rate hikes.
"Our view has been for a while now (on the) Aussie -- short term weakness, longer term strength," Bankers Trust senior economist David Bassanese said.

"Short term interest rate differentials are narrowing, but looking further out we are going to get two things late this year or early next year that should support the dollar," he said, nominating the probable commencement of a tightening cycle domestically and firming commodity prices.

Prospects of firmer growth were helped by the ANZ job advertisement series for March. Despite a 1.9 percent fall in the month, the ANZ said the series still pointed to improving labour market conditions, and the trend remained positive.

"The trend in job vacancies supports other recent data, such as retail sales and building approvals, which point to an economy on the upswing," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said in a commentary.
However, with a market focusing on more immediate rises in U.S. rates that offered little support for the local unit.
In late Sydney trade, the U.S. dollar was at 124.70/75 yen and 1.6897/02 marks, compared with New York closes at 124.27/32 and 1.6860/65.
The U.S. dollar shrugged of news of a larger than expected Japanese current account surplus, which stood at 865.2 billion yen in February, up from 750 billion a year ago.

However, it pulled back from its highs on rumours of Bank of Japan checking, and Ministry of Finance suggestions to life insurers they not buy dollar/yen, as well as options-related sales and exporter offers.
